tip.body: With vehicles you ride inside, use en: en bus, en métro, en tram, en train, en voiture. With things you go on or with your own feet, use à: à pied, à vélo (you'll also hear en vélo). tip.title: Est-ce qu'il y a … près d'ici ?
tip.body: Est-ce qu'il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ? (Is there a pharmacy near here?) works for anything you're looking for; in everyday speech people just say Il y a une pharmacie près d'ici ? with a rising voice, and il y a often sounds like "ya". Je cherche … means I'm looking for …. Useful places: la mairie (town hall), l'office de tourisme, un distributeur (cash machine — in Québec, un guichet automatique).

lessons.title: Je vais au musée
lessons.goal: Use aller + à (au, à la, à l', aux) and prepositions of place.

tip.title: à + le = au, de + le = du
tip.body: Aller (to go) is irregular: je vais, tu vas, il/elle/on va, nous allons, vous allez, ils/elles vont. "To" a place is à, and it merges with le and les: au cinéma (à + le), aux toilettes (à + les), but à la gare and à l'hôtel stay as they are. Many place words end in de, which merges the same way: à côté du parc (de + le), en face de la gare, près de l'église, à côté des magasins. Listen for the liaison in nous‿allons and vous‿allez (a z sound).

culture.title: Le métro
culture.body: The Paris métro opened in 1900 and is still the quickest way around the city; stations are announced by name, and lines are known by number and by their end station (direction La Défense). Several other cities have a métro too, including Lyon, Marseille, Lille, Toulouse and Rennes in France, as well as Brussels, Lausanne and Montréal, whose métro runs on rubber tyres. Many French cities have brought back the tram. On buses and trams you usually validate your ticket in a small machine when you board — keep it until the end of the trip, as inspectors can check it.

culture.title: Dépanneurs and Swiss trains
culture.body: In Québec, the corner shop that sells milk, bread, snacks and newspapers until late is called un dépanneur, often shortened to le dep — from dépanner, to help someone out of a fix. In Switzerland, the train is a way of life: the federal railways (CFF in French, SBB in German) are known for frequent, punctual trains that connect with buses and boats, and timetables in many places repeat at the same minutes every hour. In France and Switzerland the platform is la voie; in Belgium the national railway is the SNCB.
